lesson.title: weil & dass: the Verb Waits
lesson.subtitle: Twelve subclauses built on the two doors — verb-final, every time

hook.title: Two Doors, One Basement
hook.content: Open a subclause with weil (because) or dass (that) and the conjugated verb walks to the very end of the clause and waits there. Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich will — 'because I want-to'. Ich weiß, dass du kommst — 'that you coming-are'. This is the same verb-final habit Old English subordinate clauses loved, and German never abandoned it. weil is your while (same ancient word, new job), dass is your that — so the two doors are made of English wood; only the basement rule is new.

footnotes.title: Spoken German's weil Rule
footnotes.content: Colloquially, many Germans say weil with main-clause order — '...weil ich bin müde'. You will hear it everywhere; the written standard still wants the verb in the basement. Learn the standard, recognize the street version.

pattern.title: Build the Basement
pattern.content: Main clause first, verb in position 2: Ich weiß. Ich lerne. Then the door + subclause, verb last: ...dass du kommst. ...weil ich wandern will — watch that one: the modal will takes the very end and its infinitive wandern waits just before it, so the basement stacks: ...weil ich wandern will. Contrast the two architectures side by side: Ich kann nicht kommen (bracket) versus ..., weil ich nicht kommen kann (basement, kann at the end). Same words, different floor plan.
pattern.linguist_note: dass is the doublet of das — Old High German daȥ, Old English þæt, one word. The spelling split is purely orthographic convention, a fact the German Duden itself states.

exercises.prompt: Match each subclause sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: I know that you are coming
I am learning because I want to
I know that the dog is dark
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß, dass der Hund dunkel ist

matching_pairs.english: I am learning because I am sad
matching_pairs.german: Ich lerne, weil ich traurig bin

matching_pairs.english: She knows that I know the cat
matching_pairs.german: Sie weiß, dass ich die Katze kenne

matching_pairs.english: I am learning, because I have hope
matching_pairs.german: Ich lerne, weil ich Hoffnung habe

matching_pairs.english: I know that he is coming right away
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß, dass er gleich kommt

matching_pairs.english: I know your opinion, because I know you
matching_pairs.german: Ich kenne deine Meinung, weil ich dich kenne

exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß, dass du kommst, Ich lerne, weil ich will, Ich weiß, dass der Hund dunkel ist, Ich lerne, weil ich traurig bin, Sie weiß, dass ich die Katze kenne, Ich lerne, weil ich Hoffnung habe, Ich weiß, dass er gleich kommt, Ich kenne deine Meinung, weil ich dich kenne
exercises.meaning: I know that you are coming, I am learning because I want to, I know that the dog is dark, I am learning because I am sad, she knows that I know the cat, I am learning because I have hope, I know that he is coming right away, I know your opinion because I know you
exercises.explanation: After weil and dass the conjugated verb waits at the very end of its clause — the basement rule. kennen knows people and things; wissen knows facts — both work the doors.

exercises.prompt: Complete the basement: 'Ich weiß, dass du Deutsch _____.' (lernen, du-form)
exercises.meaning: Ich weiß, dass du Deutsch lernst
exercises.explanation: The subclause already has its subject (du), so only the verb lands at the end: lernst. Sorge has a seat too: Ich weiß, dass du Sorge hast — hast waits at the basement door.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence keeps MAIN-clause order after weil — the colloquial street version?
exercises.explanation: The standard wants müde bin (basement); street German often says bin müde. Understand both, write the standard.

exercises.prompt: Stack the basement: '..., weil ich wandern _____' (want, ich-form, very last word):
exercises.english_hint: the modal takes the last slot, infinitive just before it
exercises.meaning: ..., weil ich wandern will = ...because I want to hike
exercises.explanation: The basement stacks: infinitive wandern, then the modal will at the very end — two verbs, one exit.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.german: Ich weiß, dass er Angst hat.
exercises.natural: I know that he is afraid.
options: I know that he is afraid.
I know that he fear has.
I know that fear he has.
exercises.target_answer: I know that he fear has.
exercises.meaning: I know that he is afraid.
exercises.explanation: Read it the German way: 'I know that he fear has.' The verb hat waits in the basement of the dass-clause — and Angst is English's own loanword: fear with a German passport.

summary.outcome: Build weil and dass subclauses with verb-final order, including stacked modals.

use_example.german: Ich weiß, dass du morgen kommst.
use_example.english: I know that you are coming tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: weil and dass open the basement: the conjugated verb waits at the very end — Old English's habit, German's law.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: zu + infinitive ladders — Ich habe vor, Deutsch zu lernen: the bracket with a zu-glue.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from weil & dass: the Verb Waits (Today that is very good):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Heute ist das sehr gut" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of weil & dass: the Verb Waits without relying on short-term echo.

weil.context_translation: I learn because I want to.
weil.etymology_derivation: Not a Latin loan: a plain descendant of Proto-Germanic *hwīlō — the same word as English while. [wiktionary]

dass.context_translation: I know that you are coming.
dass.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *þat — the exact twin of English that, and a doublet of German das. [wiktionary]

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

weiß.etymology_derivation: t → ß. Also first-person of wissen (ich weiß = I know/am wise).

traurig.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz — English dreary is the cognate, with English d ↔ German t. [wiktionary]

angst.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *angustiz; the page names no English cognate (anguish/angry not cited) — treat as memorize. [wiktionary]

hoffnung.etymology_derivation: hoffen (to hope) + -ung: German hardened English p into pf-f, so hope became hoffen; the page lists English hoping as the cognate. [wiktionary]

sorge.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *surgo — the page lists English sorrow as the cognate: the same care-root that grew into sorrow. [wiktionary]

gleich.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, having the same form, built from ga- plus the ancestor of -like; the English twin is alike, and the suffix inside it is the same element as English -like and -ly. [wiktionary]

meinung.context_phrase: Meiner Meinung nach ist der Film gut.
meinung.context_translation: In my opinion the film is good.
meinung.etymology_derivation: meinen (to mean) + -ung; the page compares English meaning — your opinion is what you mean. [wiktionary]

katze.context_phrase: Die Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.
katze.context_translation: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

hund.context_phrase: Der Hund schläft auf dem Sofa.
hund.context_translation: The dog sleeps on the sofa.
hund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz — cognate with English hound, the same ancient dog-word. [wiktionary]

kennen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *kannijaną, a causative of *kunnaną (can); the page lists English ken (as in beyond my ken) — the same knowing-verb English keeps in Scotland. [wiktionary]

tier.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tior, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from PIE *dʰewsóm. English deer is the listed cognate; the Germanic d appears as t in High German. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
